query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium, as‐cast Mg-containing lightweight HEAs (with densities below 6 g/cm³), the initially homogeneous, metastable solid solution evolves during prolonged high-temperature or corrosive exposure by partitioning magnesium into discrete intermetallic precipitates (especially at grain boundaries). This phase separation disrupts the continuity and chemistry of the nascent passive film, thus altering both the corrosion kinetics and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy composed of a uniform, metastable solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled post-annealing treatment at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800°C for 24 h) and expose it to standard corrosive environments (such as 0.1 M NaCl solution) for a fixed duration.
generation.conditions: Density maintained below 6 g/cm³; oxidation tests performed in air at temperatures up to 800°C; corrosion tests conducted under standardized electrolyte (0.1 M NaCl) at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-enriched intermetallic precipitates, particularly localized along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Differences in constituent elemental properties drive atomic diffusion and exsolution from the supersaturated matrix, leading to segregated Mg-rich intermetallics. These precipitates alter the local chemical potential and disrupt the continuity of the protective oxide/passivation film, thereby modifying both the corrosion current density and the kinetics of high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous alloy, post-treated samples will exhibit a measurable increase in Mg-rich precipitate volume fraction as detected by microstructural analysis; concurrently, electrochemical tests will show higher corrosion current densities and altered oxidation weight-gain kinetics (e.g., reduced or non-uniform oxide layer formation) relative to the as-cast baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-cast condition with a uniform, metastable single-phase solid solution and established baseline corrosion and oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: All processing remains within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm³ and uses rapid induction melting to achieve the non-equilibrium state. Testing is confined to temperatures up to 800°C and corrosion in standardized NaCl solutions.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of magnesium partitioning versus possible co-partitioning of other alloying elements in the formation of stable intermetallics are not fully quantified, and the direct correlation between intermetallic formation and passivation film breakdown requires further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples via rapid induction melting to ensure a non-equilibrium, homogeneous starting state. Subject one set to no further processing (as-cast control) and the other set to annealing at 800°C for 24 hours. Expose both sets to standardized corrosion tests (immersing in 0.1 M NaCl solution for a fixed period) and perform high-temperature oxidation tests in air. Use SEM, TEM, and XRD to characterize the microstructure and to detect the presence or absence of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
measurements: Quantification of precipitate volume fraction and distribution using SEM/TEM/XRD
Potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current densities
Oxidation weight gain measurements and oxide layer morphology characterization
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess passive film integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and if their corrosion and oxidation performance parameters (corrosion current density, oxide kinetics, and passive film stability) do not differ significantly from the as-cast samples, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRecently, the design of lightweight high entropy alloys (HEAs) with a mass density lower than 5 g/cm3 has attracted much research interest in structural materials. We applied a first principles-based high-throughput method to design lightweight HEAs in single solid-solution phase. Three lightweight quinary HEA families were studied: AlBeMgTiLi, AlBeMgTiSi and AlBeMgTiCu. By comprehensively exploring their entire compositional spaces, we identified the most promising compositions according to the following design criteria: the highest stability, lowest mass density, largest elastic modulus and specific stiffness, along with highest Pugh’s ratio. We found that HEAs with the topmost compositions exhibit a negative formation energy, a low density and high specific Young’s modulus, but a low Pugh’s ratio. Importantly, we show that the most stable composition, Al0.31Be0.15Mg0.14Ti0.05Si0.35 is energetically more stable than its metallic compounds and it significantly outperforms the current lightweight engineering alloys such as the 7075 Al alloy. Microstructural Stability and Densification Behavior of Cantor-Type High-Entropy Alloy Processed by Spark Plasma Sintering

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cantor type (CoCrFeMnNi) are widely recognized as model systems for studying the relationships between composition, microstructure, and functional performance. In this study, atomized Cantor alloy powders were consolidated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under systematically varied process parameters (temperature and dwell time). The densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response were investigated using Archimedes’ density measurements, Vickers hardness testing, compression tests, scanning electron microscopy, and EDS mapping. The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times. Despite the ultrafast nature of SPS, grain growth was observed, particularly at elevated temperatures and extended dwell times, challenging the assumption that SPS inherently limits grain coarsening. On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.

Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment

Abstract: Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures.
